title: SCOT: Soft Correspondence via Optimal Transport for Multi-Source Cross-City Transfer
topic: General Machine Learning->Transfer, Multitask and Meta-learning
claim: Our method aligns source and target embeddings region-by-region while preserving structure, whereas a global-alignment baseline over-mixes heterogeneous regions.
layout: Left cartoon of 3 steps (a-c), right two t-SNE scatter plots side by side
description: The figure has two halves. On the left, a three-step cartoon shows source-city and target-city icons feeding region embeddings. Source points are dark and target points are pale, in three colored clusters: orange Region 1, blue Region 2 and green Region 3. Arrows lead to a mixed joint embedding blob in (b), then to (c), where each region's source and target points sit together in separate ellipses. On the right, two t-SNE scatter plots use blue circles for the source city and orange triangles for the target city. Panel (a), SCOT (ours), shows several separate clusters where blue and orange points overlap closely along shared structure. Panel (b), CoRE, shows one diffuse blob in which the points are mixed, and a separate orange-only cluster sits in the lower right.
caption: Illustration of motivation. Figure 2: t-SNE visualization for XA→BJ.
abstract: Cross-city transfer uses labeled data from well-instrumented cities to improve prediction in label-scarce ones. The task is difficult when cities have incompatible region partitions and no ground-truth correspondence. Existing methods either rely on heuristic anchors, which can create hubness, or align global distributions, which can over-mix heterogeneous regions. We propose SCOT (Soft Correspondence via Optimal Transport), an optimal transport-based framework for learning explicit, mass-controlled soft correspondences between unequal region sets. SCOT combines an optimal transport-weighted contrastive loss, a one-sided cycle regularizer, and a shared prototype hub for multi-source transfer. Across real-world cities and tasks, SCOT consistently outperforms strong baselines, reducing MAE and MAPE by 5-50%. Additional analyses show that the learned correspondences are selective, region-specific, and robust to heterogeneous settings.
